title: Choosing a question worth publishing
summary: Three gates for a good quantum-oncology question, the kinds of contribution that get published (including negative results), how to search the literature, and why your first collaborator should be an oncologist.

shots.title:
A question worth
publishing.
shots.subtitle: Important, quantum-shaped, testable now.
shots.narration: Most weak papers at this interface fail before any code is written: the question was wrong. Here is how to choose one that survives referees from both fields.

shots.heading: Three gates
items: **Important** — would an oncologist change a decision if you answered it?
**Quantum-shaped** — is there structure a quantum method exploits: electrons, sampling, combinatorics?
**Testable now** — can you show something honest at today's scale, or estimate tomorrow's?
shots.narration: Three gates. Is it important: would an oncologist change a decision if you answered it? Is it quantum-shaped: does it have structure a quantum method could exploit? And is it testable now, honestly, at today's scale — or estimable for tomorrow's?

right.heading: Strong
items: “Does a quantum kernel beat tuned classical kernels on subtype X — and does entanglement matter?”
“What would phase estimation cost for photosensitizer Y, versus DMRG?”

shots.narration: Compare. Weak: can quantum machine learning classify cancer? Strong: does a quantum kernel beat tuned classical kernels on one subtype task, leakage-free, and does removing entanglement change the answer? Strong questions name the comparator and the test.

shots.heading: What gets published
shots.narration: Four kinds of contribution get published here: resource estimates, like the P450 study; honest benchmarks, including negative results; workflows that connect real drug-design tasks to quantum methods; and perspectives that map where advantage could arise.

shots.text: **Negative results are publishable** when the benchmark is good — and the field needs them.
shots.narration: Negative results are publishable when the benchmark is careful. A well-designed study showing a quantum model does not beat a strong baseline is useful knowledge, and leaders in the field have argued for exactly that shift.

shots.text: Biomarker-selected trials succeed more often: **patient selection** is a high-value target for computation.
shots.narration: If you want oncologists to care, aim where value is proven. Trials that select patients by biomarker have higher success rates, so better biomarkers are a high-value target for any computational method.

shots.heading: Where to look
items: **PubMed** with MeSH terms — the oncology literature
**The Quantum Advantage Tracker** — claims and classical replies
shots.narration: Search both literatures: PubMed for oncology, arXiv for quantum methods, bioRxiv and medRxiv for preprints, and the community Quantum Advantage Tracker, where claims are posted and challenged.

shots.text: Your first collaborator should be an **oncologist or cancer biologist**: they own the question, the data access and the endpoint.
shots.narration: Finally, find your oncology collaborator early. They know which questions matter, they can get access to data, and they will tell you which endpoint a clinical referee will accept.

cards.text: Can quantum computers help with cancer?
cards.why: No task, no comparator, no test.

cards.text: Does XY-mixer QAOA find better 10-gene panels than simulated annealing, at equal wall-clock time, on three TCGA response-prediction tasks with external validation?
cards.why: Task, baseline, budget and validation are all named.

cards.text: What logical-qubit count and Toffoli depth would phase estimation need for the iron centre of CYP3A4, and how does DMRG fare on the same active spaces?
cards.why: A resource estimate with a classical comparison — a recognised paper type.

cards.text: We will run a quantum neural network on mammograms
cards.why: A method in search of a question; the classical bar is very high.

cards.text: Does removing entanglement from a published quantum-kernel cancer classifier change its accuracy?
cards.why: A focused ablation that tests a mechanism.

cards.text: Quantum AI to personalise all cancer treatment

Your first falsifiable prediction — what result would prove you wrong?

questions.prompt: Which is most likely to be publishable?
options: A quantum classifier with no baseline
A careful benchmark showing a quantum model does not beat strong classical baselines
questions.explain: Careful negative results are useful — the field needs them.

questions.prompt: Why aim computational work at patient selection?
options: Biomarker-selected trials have higher success probabilities
questions.explain: Better patient selection is where value has already been demonstrated.
